events: Khalsa Saajna Divas / Vaisakhi – Creation of Khalsa Panth
title: Vaisakhi and Khalsa Saajna Divas: the creation of the Khalsa in 1699
desc: Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur Sahib: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji asks for a head, the Panj Pyare, Khande di Pahul and the five Ks. The story of Khalsa Saajna Divas and its celebration.
alt: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib at Anandpur Sahib
cap: Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur Sahib, where the Khalsa was created
body: Vaisakhi is the harvest festival of Punjab, but for Sikhs it is above all Khalsa Saajna Divas, the day in 1699 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji created the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib. It is one of the most important days of the Sikh year, celebrated by Sikhs across the world.
## A sword and a question

The Guru called Sikhs from far and wide to Anandpur Sahib for Vaisakhi, and a vast sangat gathered on the hill where Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib now stands. The Guru came out with a drawn sword and asked who would give his head for the faith. A silence fell. Then Daya Ram of Lahore stood up. The Guru took him into a tent and came out with his sword dripping, asking for another. One by one, Dharam Das, Himmat Rai, Mohkam Chand and Sahib Chand came forward, from different castes and corners of India.
## The Panj Pyare and the Amrit

The Guru brought all five out, dressed alike, and called them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. He prepared Amrit in an iron bowl, stirring water with a double-edged sword, the khanda, while reciting the banis, and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji added sugar crystals. He gave them Khande di Pahul, named each of them Singh, gave them the five Ks, the articles of faith beginning with kes, the uncut hair, and a code of discipline. Then he knelt before them and asked them to give Amrit to him, joining the Khalsa he had created.
## How Vaisakhi is celebrated

Sikhs mark the day with Akhand Paath, Nagar Kirtans led by five Singhs dressed as the Panj Pyare, Amrit Sanchar ceremonies, kirtan and langar. The Nishan Sahib at many gurdwaras is taken down, washed and given a new cloth. The largest gatherings are at Anandpur Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, and at Sri Harmandir Sahib.

title: Bandi Chhor Divas: why Sikhs celebrate on Diwali
desc: Bandi Chhor Divas remembers the release of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji from Gwalior Fort with fifty-two kings holding his cloak. The story and the lights of Amritsar.
alt: Sri Harmandir Sahib and its sarovar
cap: Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, lit up every year on Bandi Chhor Divas
body: Bandi Chhor Divas, the Day of Liberation, falls on the same day as Diwali. Sikhs celebrate it in memory of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, who refused to leave his imprisonment in the fort of Gwalior unless fifty-two kings held with him were set free too.
## The Guru at Gwalior

Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, built Sri Akal Takht Sahib and raised a body of armed Sikhs, and the emperor Jahangir grew wary of him. On a pretext, which tradition links to an unpaid fine imposed on his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the Guru was held in the fort of Gwalior, where many princes were kept as political prisoners. Sikhs came from Punjab to bow at the walls of the fort, and the Guru's presence comforted the other prisoners.
## The cloak of fifty-two tassels

When Jahangir ordered the Guru's release, the Guru refused to go unless the fifty-two kings imprisoned with him were also freed. The emperor, thinking few could escape, said that as many as could hold on to the Guru's cloak might leave with him. The Guru had a cloak made with fifty-two tassels, and every king walked out holding one. He became known as the Bandi Chhor, the liberator of prisoners. Gurdwara Data Bandi Chhor Sahib now stands at Gwalior Fort.
## The lights of Amritsar

When the Guru reached Amritsar, the city lit lamps to welcome him. The tradition continues: on Bandi Chhor Divas, Sri Harmandir Sahib and the whole complex are lit with lamps and candles, fireworks light the sky over the sarovar, and sangats fill the parikarma. In gurdwaras and homes everywhere, Sikhs light lamps, hold kirtan and Ardas, and share sweets.

events: Nanakshahi Samvat 559 / Sikh New Year (Chet Sangrand)
title: Sikh New Year: Nanakshahi Samvat 559 begins on 1 Chet
name: Sikh New Year – Nanakshahi 559
desc: The Nanakshahi year 559 begins on 1 Chet, 14 March 2027. What the Nanakshahi calendar is, how its years are counted from 1469, and how the Sikh New Year is kept.
body: The Sikh New Year falls on 1 Chet, the first day of the first month of the Nanakshahi calendar. On 14 March 2027 the year 559 begins. The day is also the Sangrand of Chet, the start of the new solar month.
## The Nanakshahi calendar

The Nanakshahi calendar counts its years from 1469, the year of the birth of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, so the year that runs from March 2026 to March 2027 is 558. Its twelve months carry the old Punjabi names, from Chet and Vaisakh to Magh and Phagan, the same months the Gurus used in the Barah Maha compositions of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. A version of the calendar designed by Pal Singh Purewal was adopted by the SGPC in 2003, with months of fixed length; it was later amended, and today the SGPC's calendar keeps fixed solar dates for some days and follows the moon for others, such as the Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Hazri's calendar follows the SGPC's for 558.
## The Barah Maha

Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji in Raag Tukhari and Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Raag Maajh each composed a Barah Maha, a song of the twelve months, in which the changing seasons mirror the longing of the soul for the Divine. Chet, the month of spring, opens both. At the Sangrand of each month, many gurdwaras recite the part of the Barah Maha for that month.
## How the day is observed

Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas, and for the recital of the Barah Maha of Chet. Many Sikhs begin the year by rising at Amrit Vela and resolving to keep their Nitnem through the year ahead. Hazri adds the calendar for each new year before it begins.

events: Sri Muktsar Sahib Jorh Mela / Shaheedi Divas
title: Maghi at Sri Muktsar Sahib: Mai Bhago Ji and the Chali Mukte
name: Sri Muktsar Sahib Jorh Mela – Chali Mukte
desc: The battle of Khidrana, where forty Singhs led by Mai Bhago Ji returned to fight for the Guru, and the torn disclaimer of Bhai Mahan Singh. The Maghi mela at Muktsar.
alt: Gurdwara Tuti Gandhi Sahib at Sri Muktsar Sahib
cap: Gurdwara Tuti Gandhi Sahib, Sri Muktsar Sahib, where the broken tie was mended
body: Sri Muktsar Sahib remembers the battle of Khidrana in 1705, where forty Singhs who had once deserted Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji came back and gave their lives for him, and were blessed as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones. The SGPC's calendar keeps two days: a Shaheedi Divas in spring, and the great Jorh Mela on Maghi, the first day of Magh.
## The disclaimer

During the long siege of Anandpur Sahib, a group of Sikhs from the Majha, worn down by hunger, told the Guru they wished to leave. He asked them to write that they were no longer his Sikhs, and forty signed the disclaimer, the bedava, and went home. There they were met with scorn. Mai Bhago Ji, a woman of Jhabal, shamed them for leaving the Guru in his hour of need and led them back to find him, riding at their head.
## Khidrana

They caught up with the Guru in the dry Malwa near the pool of Khidrana, with a Mughal army in pursuit. Taking position at the water, the forty and Mai Bhago Ji fought off the attack while the Guru shot arrows from a nearby mound. The army withdrew, but all forty fell, and Mai Bhago Ji was wounded.
## The torn page

Walking among the fallen, the Guru found one Singh, Bhai Mahan Singh, still alive, and took his head in his lap. Bhai Mahan Singh asked him to tear up the disclaimer. The Guru took it out and tore it, and Bhai Mahan Singh died in peace. The Guru blessed the forty as the Chali Mukte, and Khidrana became Muktsar, the pool of liberation.
## The Jorh Mela
Every Maghi, vast sangats gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib to bathe in the sarovar and for kirtan, Ardas and a great Nagar Kirtan. Every Ardas remembers the forty.

events: Jorh Mela – Baba Bakala Sahib / Guru Ladho Re
title: Rakhar Puniya Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib: Guru Ladho Re
name: Jorh Mela – Baba Bakala Sahib
desc: The Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib on Rakhar Puniya remembers how Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana found Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji and cried Guru ladho re. The mela and its story.
cap: Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib, Amritsar district
body: The Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib, held on Rakhar Puniya, the full moon of Sawan, remembers the day in 1664 when Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana found the true Guru among many claimants at Bakala, and called out to the sangat: Guru ladho re, I have found the Guru. It is one of the largest melas of the Majha.
## Twenty-two Gurus at Bakala

Before his Joti Jot in Delhi, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, a town near the Beas. Twenty-two members of the Sodhi family hurried to set up seats there, each claiming the Guruship. Meanwhile, Tegh Bahadur Ji, the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, lived quietly at Bakala in meditation, in a room below the ground, making no claim at all.
## The test of the coins

Bhai Makhan Shah, a Lubana trader, had prayed to the Guru when his ship was in a storm and vowed five hundred gold coins if he reached shore. At Bakala he put two coins before each claimant and waited. Each accepted the two and blessed him. Then he was told of one more holy man, and found Tegh Bahadur Ji, who asked why he was offering two coins when he had promised five hundred, and showed the mark on his shoulder where he had pushed the ship to safety. Makhan Shah climbed onto a roof and called the sangat to their Guru.
## The mela

Gurdwara Baba Bakala Sahib, with Gurdwara Bhora Sahib at the place of the underground room, draws sangats from across Punjab for the mela, with kirtan, katha, Ardas and langar. Read the story of [the Gurgaddi of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji](/gurpurab/gurgaddi-purab-guru-tegh-bahadur-ji).

events: Jorh Mela Gurdwara Kandh Sahib / Marriage of Guru Nanak Dev Ji
title: Kandh Sahib, Batala: the marriage of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Mata Sulakhani Ji
name: Jorh Mela – Kandh Sahib, Batala
desc: Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji married Mata Sulakhani Ji at Batala in 1487. The wall of Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, Gurdwara Dehra Sahib, and the Jorh Mela held in Batala every year.
cap: Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, Batala, where the mud wall is preserved
body: The Jorh Mela at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala, Gurdaspur district, remembers the marriage of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Mata Sulakhani Ji, which tradition places in 1487. It is the largest annual gathering in Batala, a celebration as much as a remembrance.
## The wedding at Batala

Mata Sulakhani Ji was the daughter of Bhai Mool Chand Chona, a Khatri of Pakhoke Randhawa, who was living at Batala. The young Nanak, then working at Sultanpur Lodhi, came to Batala with his wedding party, accompanied by his family and friends. Tradition remembers that the bride's family, being followers of old customs, were uneasy that the groom would not perform all the usual rituals, and that some of them argued with the Guru.
## The wall that did not fall

The wedding party was seated beside an old mud wall, and tradition remembers that some hoped it would fall on the Guru. An old woman warned him that the wall was about to collapse; the Guru answered calmly that it would stand for ages to come. A part of that mud wall, the kandh, is still preserved under glass at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib, which takes its name from it. Gurdwara Dehra Sahib in Batala marks the place where the wedding ceremony was held.
## Family life

Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Mata Sulakhani Ji had two sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. The Guru's marriage is often recalled as part of his teaching that the spiritual life is lived within the family, not by renouncing it.
## The Jorh Mela
The mela is held each year with Nagar Kirtan recreating the wedding procession from Sultanpur Lodhi, kirtan, Ardas and langar.

events: Annual Chola Sahib Jorh Mela – Dera Baba Nanak (supplementary cross-check)
title: Chola Sahib Jorh Mela at Dera Baba Nanak: the cloak of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
name: Chola Sahib Jorh Mela – Dera Baba Nanak
desc: Gurdwara Chola Sahib at Dera Baba Nanak keeps a cloak believed to have been given to Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on his travels. Its story, Dera Baba Nanak, and the March mela.
body: The Chola Sahib Jorh Mela is held each year in early March at Dera Baba Nanak, in Gurdaspur district, close to the border with Pakistan. It centres on the Chola Sahib, a cloak kept at the gurdwara of that name and believed by tradition to have been given to Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on his travels to the west.
## The Chola Sahib

The Chola Sahib is a long cloak covered in writing in Arabic script, with verses and names in praise of the Divine. Tradition holds that it was presented to Guru Nanak Dev Ji by admirers during his udasi to the lands of Islam, often said to be at Baghdad or Mecca, as a mark of the respect in which he was held. It was kept by the Guru's descendants and later came to Dera Baba Nanak, where it is shown to the sangat at the mela. Historians have discussed its origin and its inscriptions, and sangats regard it with deep reverence.
## Dera Baba Nanak

Dera Baba Nanak stands on the Indian side of the Ravi, across the river from Kartarpur, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years. After his passing, his family settled here, and the town grew around the dera of the Guru's descendants. Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in the town is associated with the Guru's visits. Since 2019 the Kartarpur Corridor has begun here, letting pilgrims cross without a visa to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, a few kilometres away.
## The Jorh Mela

For several days the town fills with sangats for kirtan, Ardas and langar, and for the showing of the Chola Sahib. Many pilgrims also visit the viewing platform from which Kartarpur Sahib can be seen across the border.

title: Miri-Piri Divas: the two swords of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
desc: Miri-Piri Divas remembers the two swords of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, for worldly and spiritual authority, and the balance at the heart of Sikh life. The day explained.
alt: Sri Akal Takht Sahib in the 1920s
cap: Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, in the 1920s
body: Miri-Piri Divas remembers the teaching of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, who wore two swords: one of Miri, worldly authority and responsibility, and one of Piri, spiritual authority. The day reminds Sikhs that devotion and the duty to stand up for justice belong together.
## The two swords

When Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became Guru in 1606, after the martyrdom of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, he put aside the seli, the woollen cord worn by the earlier Gurus, and girded himself with two swords. He built Sri Akal Takht Sahib facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, kept horses and armed Sikhs, and asked Sikhs to bring weapons as offerings. The Sikhs, who had seen their Guru tortured to death, learned to defend themselves and others.
## Saint and soldier

Tradition remembers a meeting between the Guru and Samarth Ramdas, the Maratha saint, who asked how a follower of Guru Nanak could carry weapons and ride like a king. The Guru is remembered as answering that he was a householder outwardly and a renunciate within, that the sword was to protect the poor and destroy the tyrant, and that Guru Nanak had renounced not the world but the self. The idea was carried forward by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji in the Khalsa, the saint-soldier, and the Khanda, the Sikh emblem, includes two curved swords for Miri and Piri.
## How the day is observed
Gurdwaras hold kirtan, katha and Ardas, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and many hold displays of gatka. It is a day to think about how faith shapes the way one acts in the world.

events: Sikh Dastaar Divas / World Sikh Turban Day
title: Sikh Dastaar Divas: the meaning of the turban on World Sikh Turban Day
desc: Dastaar Divas, kept the day before Vaisakhi, celebrates the Sikh turban: why Sikhs wear it, what it means, and how turban-tying camps mark the day around the world.
alt: A Sikh man wearing a turban
cap: The dastaar, worn by Sikhs as a crown of faith
body: Sikh Dastaar Divas, also called World Sikh Turban Day, is kept on the day before Vaisakhi, when the Khalsa was created in 1699. It celebrates the dastaar, the Sikh turban, and invites people of every background to learn what it means, and sometimes to try one on.
## Why Sikhs wear the dastaar

Kes, uncut hair, is the first of the five Ks that Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji gave the Khalsa, and the dastaar covers and protects it. In the India of the Gurus' time, a turban was worn by kings and nobles, and the low castes were forbidden to wear one. The Gurus gave it to every Sikh, man or woman, as a sign that all are equal and sovereign under the Guru, and as a reminder to live up to that dignity. A Sikh's turban is treated with respect, and tying it each morning is part of the day's discipline.
## A visible faith

The dastaar makes a Sikh recognisable anywhere, which the Guru intended: a Sikh could not hide in a crowd and was expected to stand up for those in need. Sikhs have often had to defend the right to wear it, in schools, workplaces and armies, and many have been targeted because of it. Dastaar Divas grew out of efforts by Sikh organisations in the 2000s to build that understanding.
## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras and Sikh groups hold turban-tying camps for children and young people, competitions in tying the dastaar, and stalls in public places where anyone can have a turban tied and learn about it. In Punjab many schools and colleges take part.

title: Independence Day and the Sikhs: sacrifice in India's freedom struggle
desc: Why the SGPC's calendar marks 15 August: the part Sikhs played in India's freedom struggle, from the Kukas and the Ghadar Party to Jallianwala Bagh and the Akali morchas.
body: India became independent on 15 August 1947, and the SGPC's calendar marks the day. For Sikhs, it is a day to remember the very large part their community played in the freedom struggle, and also, because independence came with the Partition of Punjab, a day of mixed memory.
## A share far beyond their numbers

Sikhs were less than two percent of India's people, yet they were heavily represented among those hanged, imprisoned and transported for the freedom struggle. The Kuka or Namdhari movement under Baba Ram Singh resisted British rule from the 1860s, and many Kukas were blown from cannon at Malerkotla in 1872. The Ghadar Party, founded in 1913 by Indians on the Pacific coast of America, most of them Punjabi Sikhs, sent hundreds home to raise a revolt; Kartar Singh Sarabha and many others were hanged. Bhagat Singh came from a Sikh family steeped in the struggle.
## Jallianwala Bagh and the morchas

The massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on Vaisakhi in 1919, where hundreds were killed, many of them pilgrims, turned much of India against British rule. The non-violent morchas of the Gurdwara Reform Movement in the early 1920s, at Guru Ka Bagh, Jaito and over the keys of the Toshakhana, were among the first mass campaigns to force the government's hand. Sikh soldiers in the Indian National Army, and leaders such as Baba Kharak Singh and Master Tara Singh, also played their part.
## How the day is observed

Many gurdwaras hold Ardas for those who gave their lives for freedom. The next day, the SGPC's calendar remembers the people of Punjab killed in the Partition. Read about [the Partition Ardas day](/gurpurab/partition-1947-ardas-day).

events: Ardas Day for Punjabis killed during the 1947 Partition
title: Ardas for the Punjabis killed in the 1947 Partition
desc: The day after Independence, the SGPC's calendar remembers the Punjabis of every faith killed in the Partition of 1947, and the Sikh shrines left behind in Pakistan.
body: On the day after India's Independence, the SGPC's calendar keeps an Ardas Day for the Punjabis who were killed during the Partition of 1947. It remembers the people of Punjab, Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims alike, who lost their lives, their homes and their land when the province was divided between India and Pakistan.
## A divided Punjab

The new border, announced only after independence, ran through the heart of Punjab. Lahore, the capital of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, went to Pakistan, and so did Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Kartarpur, where he spent his last years, Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore, Panja Sahib, and hundreds of other places sacred to the Sikhs, along with much of the fertile canal land that Sikh farmers had settled.
## The killing and the migration

In the months around August 1947 Punjab was swept by communal violence. Trains arrived full of the dead, villages were burned, and women were abducted or killed, some by their own families to save them from capture. Estimates of the dead across the subcontinent run from several hundred thousand to two million, and Punjab bore the greatest share. Some ten million people crossed the new border in one of the largest migrations in history. Nearly every Sikh family from West Punjab carries stories of what was lost.
## The daily Ardas

Since 1947 the Sikh Ardas has included a prayer for free access to, and care of, the gurdwaras and shrines from which the Panth has been separated. The opening of the Kartarpur Corridor in 2019 answered part of that prayer.
## How the day is observed
Gurdwaras hold Ardas for all those killed, and many families remember the villages and homes their parents and grandparents left behind.

title: Punjabi Suba Day: the formation of Punjab state on 1 November 1966
desc: On 1 November 1966 Punjab was reorganised as a Punjabi-speaking state after the long Punjabi Suba movement. The movement, its leaders, and what was left unsettled.
body: Punjabi Suba Day marks 1 November 1966, when the state of Punjab was reorganised on the basis of language, creating a Punjabi-speaking state. It was the result of the Punjabi Suba movement, one of the longest political campaigns in the history of the state, in which Sikhs played the leading part.
## States by language

After independence, India began to redraw its states along the lines of language, and in 1956 many new linguistic states were formed. The demand for a Punjabi-speaking state, where Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script would be the language of government and schooling, was set aside. The Shiromani Akali Dal, under Master Tara Singh and later Sant Fateh Singh, led the campaign for it.
## The movement

Through the 1950s and 1960s, tens of thousands of volunteers courted arrest in morchas, and in 1955 police entered the complex of Sri Harmandir Sahib to arrest protesters. Leaders went on fasts unto death. After the war of 1965, in which Punjab and its soldiers bore much of the burden, the central government agreed to reorganise the state.
## The reorganisation of 1966

On 1 November 1966 the old Punjab was divided: the Hindi-speaking south became Haryana, the hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh, and Chandigarh, the capital, was made a union territory shared by Punjab and Haryana. The questions of Chandigarh, of Punjabi-speaking areas left outside the state, and of river waters remained unsettled, and came back in the demands of later years.
## How the day is observed
The day is marked with events celebrating Punjabi language and culture, and in some gurdwaras with Ardas for those who took part in the movement.

title: SGPC Foundation Day: how the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee began
desc: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee was formed at Sri Akal Takht Sahib on 15 November 1920 to free the gurdwaras from the mahants. Its history and its work today.
body: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the SGPC, was founded on 15 November 1920 at a gathering at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. It was formed to bring the historic gurdwaras of the Sikhs under the management of the Panth itself, and today it manages Sri Harmandir Sahib and many other gurdwaras.
## The gurdwaras under the mahants

In the nineteenth century, many historic gurdwaras had passed into the hands of hereditary mahants, who ran them as private property and often allowed practices contrary to the Gurus' teaching. Sri Harmandir Sahib itself was run by a manager appointed by the British government. Early in the twentieth century, the Singh Sabha movement had revived Sikh learning and identity, and a demand grew for the Panth to manage its own shrines.
## A committee of the Panth

In October 1920 a group of Sikhs from castes the priests treated as low came to Sri Harmandir Sahib with an offering, which the priests refused. The sangat took a hukam from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, which welcomed them; the priests fled, and the Sikhs took charge of Sri Akal Takht Sahib. A month later, a large gathering formed a committee of 175 members to manage the gurdwaras, the SGPC. Within weeks the Shiromani Akali Dal was formed to organise volunteers.
## The reform movement

The years that followed saw the morchas at Nankana Sahib, Guru Ka Bagh, Jaito and over the keys of the Toshakhana. The movement ended with the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925, which gave the SGPC legal charge of the historic gurdwaras of Punjab, with its members elected by Sikh voters.
## Its work today
The SGPC manages gurdwaras, runs schools, colleges and hospitals, publishes Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and sets the Nanakshahi calendar that Hazri follows.

title: Shiromani Akali Dal Foundation Day: from the jathas of 1920 to a political party
desc: The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded on 14 December 1920 to organise volunteers for the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Its origins in the morchas and its later history.
body: The Shiromani Akali Dal was founded on 14 December 1920, a month after the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. The SGPC's calendar keeps its foundation day because of the place the Akali Dal held in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, the struggle to bring the historic gurdwaras into the Panth's own hands.
## The Akali jathas

The word akali means a follower of the Timeless One, Akal, and recalls the Akali Nihangs of the eighteenth century, who served the Panth and guarded its shrines. In 1920, as Sikhs began to take over gurdwaras from the mahants, local bands of volunteers called Akali jathas formed across Punjab. The Shiromani Akali Dal was created to coordinate them as a central body, with Sardar Sarmukh Singh Jhabal as its first president.
## The morchas

Akali volunteers carried the weight of the reform movement. They faced the massacre at Nankana Sahib in 1921, the beatings at Guru Ka Bagh in 1922, and the firing at Jaito in 1924, keeping to their pledge of non-violence. Their sacrifices led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925 and earned the respect of the national movement.
## A political party

After 1925 the Akali Dal became the main political voice of the Sikhs. It led the Punjabi Suba movement, which created the Punjabi-speaking state in 1966, opposed the Emergency of 1975, and led the Dharam Yudh Morcha of the 1980s. It has formed governments in Punjab several times. Today there are several groups claiming the Akali name, and views of the party's record differ, as with any political body.
## How the day is observed
The day is marked with Ardas and gatherings, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib.
